(VERBATIM)
"Free" wins on paper even when it costs more in people. The tool is a rounding error next to salaries.

[click] 
Leadership — the most resourced option. Who can we staff to support this, and how do we model our organization for it.

## Thesis: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*A language migration should optimize for the easiest option for the person who has to write the code.*
:::

::: {.fragment}
*For them, the hard part was never the syntax. It's keeping the way they think.*
:::

::: {.notes}
[click]
(VERBATIM, SLOWLY)
A language migration should optimize for the easiest option for the person who has to write the code.
Easier than cheapest, than best-staffed, than most-compatible, than most-secure.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
And "easiest" for that person is specific. Learning new syntax is easy. Porting the mental model — for us, the tidy model — was the real challenge.
That sentence is the whole talk.
:::

## Two words {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Language]{.accent}: anything you think in — R, Python, dplyr, Polars, SQL
- [API]{.accent}: the function signature — `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)`
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Two words to fence, quickly.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
"Language" means anything you think in. R and Python, obviously. But dplyr is a language. Polars is a language. SQL is a language. You can be fluent or lost in any of them — so dplyr to Polars is a language migration, even though it's also R to Python.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
"API" means the function signature — what you pass in, what you get back. Not a web API. Every language exposes one; humans do too, it's called the five senses. The only question is whether it's easy to interact with.
Hold onto that word — it comes back as pillar one.
:::

# What "easiest" actually means {background-color="#158158"}

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM) My thesis called for optimizing for the "easiest" migration options. This is what I mean.
:::

## Pillar one: the syntax is the easy part {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Early]{.accent} wins

- The [thin-slice]{.accent} effect
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Pillar one. The abstract for this talk says "learning new syntax is easy" — and it is, if you pick the option where the API is close to the one you already know.
The test: can the Data Scientist be productive immediately?

[click] 
Early wins — real code that runs on day one, before anyone has
mastered environments, classes, or types. 

Impresses superiors; feels good to accomplish things.

[click] 
Thin-slice theory, a well established psychological phenomenom:
First impressions aren't accurate, but they have more predictive power and persistence than we'd like. We're judgemental
animals. 

Callback: my first ten minutes installing Python was that thin slice. Everyone has had that, and it's not limited to programming, obviously.

Not fair, but real, and it has to be managed.
:::

## {.code-stack}

::: {.fragment}
**dplyr**

```{.r}
library(dplyr)
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  mutate(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, "cust"),
    revenue = rowSums(across(starts_with("rev")))
  )
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Polars**

```{.python}
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c
df.filter(c.status == "paid").with_columns(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains("cust"),
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with("rev")),
)
```
:::

::: {.aside}
For the full verb-by-verb pairing, see Michael Thomas, *Building Multilingual Data Science Teams*, posit::conf(2025) — a good talk on exactly this.
:::

::: {.notes}
[click] 
dplyr for instance is a pipeline-based expressions friendly dataframe DSL.

[click] 
In Polars, we get the main verbs 1:1. Let's walk it verb by verb.

(ASIDE) There's a good posit::conf talk from Michael Thomas at Ketchbrook that does this pairing in depth — linked in the show notes.
:::

## {.code-stack transition="none"}

**dplyr**

```{.r code-line-numbers="3"}
library(dplyr)
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  mutate(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, "cust"),
    revenue = rowSums(across(starts_with("rev")))
  )
```

**Polars**

```{.python code-line-numbers="3"}
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c
df.filter(c.status == "paid").with_columns(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains("cust"),
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with("rev")),
)
```

::: {.notes}
Filter. Same verb, same predicate. The pipe became a dot.
:::

## {.code-stack transition="none"}

**dplyr**

```{.r code-line-numbers="4-5"}
library(dplyr)
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  mutate(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, "cust"),
    revenue = rowSums(across(starts_with("rev")))
  )
```

**Polars**

```{.python code-line-numbers="3-4"}
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c
df.filter(c.status == "paid").with_columns(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains("cust"),
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with("rev")),
)
```

::: {.notes}
Add a column from a string test. `mutate` became `with_columns`; `str_detect` became `.str.contains`. The Data Scientist reads this without a manual.
:::

## {.code-stack transition="none"}

**dplyr**

```{.r code-line-numbers="6"}
library(dplyr)
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  mutate(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, "cust"),
    revenue = rowSums(across(starts_with("rev")))
  )
```

**Polars**

```{.python code-line-numbers="5"}
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c
df.filter(c.status == "paid").with_columns(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains("cust"),
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with("rev")),
)
```

::: {.notes}
Sum across a rule-selected set of columns. `across(starts_with)` became a selector, `rowSums` became `sum_horizontal`. New name, same sentence.
:::

## {.code-stack transition="none"}

**dplyr**

```{.r code-line-numbers="1"}
library(dplyr)
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  mutate(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, "cust"),
    revenue = rowSums(across(starts_with("rev")))
  )
```

**Polars**

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2"}
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c
df.filter(c.status == "paid").with_columns(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains("cust"),
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with("rev")),
)
```

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = it works in ten minutes.**
:::

::: {.notes}
The imports. The star import — yes, it's an anti-pattern. We don't care yet — the DS persona doesn't care about LSPs and typing on day one.
Same with attribute access on `c`. Might annoy the type checker later. Later.

[click] 
An easy test, if your data scientists can get it in 10 minutes then it might be a good choice.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*Day one decides whether people keep going.*
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Day one decides whether people keep going.

(VERBATIM)
Everyone has a tool that lost them on day one, and they never went back.
Comfort first, control later. The fancy stuff is still there when they're ready.

(TIE-BACK, VERBATIM)
That's pillar one: the syntax — the API — is the easy part. Pick the option where day one works.
:::

## Pillar two: the mental model is the migration {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Syntax is a [lookup]{.accent}
- The mental model is [yours]{.accent}
:::

::: {.notes}
(LEAD-IN, VERBATIM)
So the syntax is easy. Then why did moving to Python feel like losing a native language — to me, and to every colleague I've asked?
Because day one is one day. Most of the Data Scientist's days are day two through day two thousand, and on those days what matters isn't the syntax. It's whether they still get to think the way they think.
Pillar two: the mental model is the actual migration.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Syntax is a lookup. You forget a verb, you search it, you move on.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
The mental model is yours. It's how you decompose a problem before you type anything. If the new option takes that away, you're not migrating — you're starting over.
For us, that model is the tidy model. We didn't pick Polars for its syntax; we picked it because the tidy way of thinking came with us.

(SIGNPOST, VERBATIM)
Three slides. First: what the tidy model actually is, in three ideas. Then two examples of what it looks like when it does — and doesn't — carry over.
:::

## What actually carries over {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Vectorized]{.accent}: think in columns, not rows
- [Functional]{.accent}: expressions are values you compose
- [Declarative]{.accent}: say what, not how
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Three ideas in the tidy model. If the new option keeps all three, the Data Scientist keeps their whole head.

[click]
Vectorized — the unit of thought is the column. You never write the row loop; the engine does.

[click]
Functional — `col("x") * 1.1` is a value. You can name it, pass it, build it up. No mutable object you have to keep in your head.

[click]
Declarative — you say what the result is, and the engine decides how. That's the pipe, the chain, the query plan.

(VERBATIM)
These are the same three ideas behind SQL and behind dplyr, which is why everyone in this room already has them.
The opposite is imperative: allocate, loop, mutate, return. Every one of those is a thing to learn and a place to be wrong.

(TIE-BACK, VERBATIM)
So when I say "easiest," this is the test for pillar two — not the syntax, the three ideas. Does the new option keep all three?
:::

## Same thought, class-first

::: {.fragment}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**dplyr**

```r
df |> filter(status == "paid")
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Polars**

```python
df.filter(c.status == "paid")
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The detour**

```java
public class Order implements Serializable {
  private String status;
  private double revenue;
  // getters, setters, no-arg constructor ...
}
Dataset<Order> orders = df.as(Encoders.bean(Order.class));
Dataset<Order> paid = orders.filter(
  (FilterFunction<Order>) o -> o.getStatus().equals("paid")
);
```
:::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = the data shows up before the type system does.**
:::

::: {.notes}
[click]
One line. Same sentence in both languages — filter the rows where status is paid.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
And here's the same filter, class-first. This is Spark's typed API in Java.
Nothing here is wrong — Java is a language where the type system shows up before the data does.
But look at what the Data Scientist has to know before the first line runs:
a class, serialization, encoders, generics, and a cast on the lambda.

That's not a Spark problem. Any class-first option carries this tax on day one.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
The data shows up before the type system. That's the easy option.

(VERBATIM)
None of that scaffolding is about the data — it's about the language. The typed API pays off later, and later is fine. But the Data Scientist wants to see rows, not write getters.

(TIE-BACK, VERBATIM)
That's the thesis in one picture: the easiest option is the one where the data shows up first.
:::

## Same thought, every column {.code-stack}

::: {.fragment}
**dplyr**

```r
df |>
  mutate(across(
    starts_with("rev"), \(x) x * 1.1
  ))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Polars**

```python
import polars.selectors as cs
df.with_columns(cs.starts_with("rev") * 1.1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The detour**

```python
for col in df.columns:
    if col.startswith("rev"):
        df[col] = df[col] * 1.1
```
:::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = you didn't learn a new way to think.**
:::

::: {.notes}
[click] dplyr — pick columns by a rule, apply one expression to all.

[click] Polars — same idea. `cs` is Polars' column selectors. The chain is the pipe; the expression is the thing inside `across`.

[click] 
(VERBATIM)
And this is the detour. Same result. Nobody's wrong.
But the Data Scientist just had to stop thinking in columns and start thinking in loops.
That's not a library problem — any language can make you write this. It's what happens when the option you chose doesn't carry your old sentence.

[click] 
The vectorized mental model came with us. That's the property to look for:
the option where your old sentences still parse.

(VERBATIM)
And there's a team version of this: when everyone writes it the same way, code review works again. Shared idioms mean the team had one migration, not eight private ones.

(TIE-BACK, VERBATIM)
That's pillar two: the mental model is the migration, and ours came with us. Nobody had to learn a new way to think.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Some days, you don't need to learn anything new.
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Migration is already information overload. It doesn't all have to land on day one. You don't take Calc 4 before Calc 1.

(VERBATIM)
Typing, classes, magic methods, the finer things a language has to offer — once people are comfortable, they go find those on their own, and they make better decisions about them than you would have made for them.
:::

## Two pillars, one thesis {.center}

::: {.pillars}
[Syntax is easy]{.accent} · [The mental model is the migration]{.accent}
:::

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Productivity
:::

::: {.fragment .big-word}
→ Familiarity
:::

::: {.fragment .big-word}
→ Confidence
:::

::: {.notes}
(CONTEXT, VERBATIM)
Let me bring this back to the thesis. A migration should optimize for the easiest option for the person who has to write the code.
I said "easiest" means two things. Pillar one: the syntax is the easy part — day one works. Pillar two: the mental model is the migration — they keep the tidy way of thinking.
Here's what you get when you have both.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Productivity — the syntax is easy, day one works. That's pillar one.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Familiarity — the mental model carries over. That's pillar two.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Confidence — and confidence is the thing a migration actually runs on.
The quiet part is talent. Good teams are made of talent, and low morale is how you lose it. Choose the easiest option and you keep both.
:::

# Ask the Data Scientist {background-color="#158158"}

## Next time you're in that room {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Ask: *does it work on [day one]{.accent}?*
- Ask: *does my old [sentence]{.accent} still parse?*
- Ask: *who [asked]{.accent} the Data Scientist?*
:::

::: {.notes}
(CONTEXT, VERBATIM)
So here's what I'd like you to take out of this room. At some point you're going to be in that migration meeting — or you'll be the assignee who found out afterward.
Finance, leadership, tech, and cyber will all have an opinion, and every one of those opinions is legitimate. Yours is too. Three questions to bring.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Day one. Can someone write real, useful code before they've mastered environments and types? Not a toy — something they'd actually ship. If it takes a week to get to the first row, that's your answer.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Old sentence. Take the one line you write every week. For me it's this:
"filter the paid rows, flag the customers, sum the revenue columns" — the line from the day-one slide.
In Polars that sentence still parses. In the class-first example it needed a class, an encoder, and a cast before I could say it.
If your everyday sentence needs a detour in the new language, that's your answer.

[click]
(VERBATIM)
Who asked the Data Scientist? Look at the assignee field. If the answer is "no one," you're the one who has to.
:::
